opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, for me it came down to a few things. When I was in school, I spent a lot of time building RL infrastructure, first Tianshou and then EnvPool, and what I kept noticing was that the bottleneck in reinforcement learning usually wasn't some clever new algorithm. It was engineering: how fast you can run environments, how cleanly you can scale training, how quickly you can iterate. OpenAI was one of the few places that seemed to really understand that and take it seriously.

The second thing was ambition. A lot of academic RL at the time was about squeezing a few more points out of Atari or MuJoCo benchmarks. That's useful, but it felt a bit disconnected from the real world. OpenAI was trying to apply RL to things that actually matter at scale, like large language models. When I saw that RL from human feedback could make a model genuinely more useful to people, that was very exciting to me. It felt like the place where RL could finally leave toy problems behind.

And third, the people and the culture. It's a relatively small group of very strong people, and there's not much hierarchy. If you have an idea and can build it, you can just go do it. As someone who likes writing code and building systems, that kind of environment, where good infrastructure is valued as much as research ideas, was exactly what I was looking for.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenAI took RL engineering seriously and contrasts its real-world ambitions with academic benchmark work, but it does not describe an ad hoc approach in small university research groups or say Weng hoped to learn a different methodology at OpenAI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it really came down to a few things. First, the people. OpenAI had a lot of the folks whose work I'd been reading and building on for years, especially on the RL side, and the chance to sit next to them and argue about ideas every day was hard to pass up.

Second, the scale. When I was working on Tianshou as a student, I spent a lot of time thinking about how to make RL training fast and reliable, but always on a handful of GPUs. At OpenAI the question flips. You're not asking "can I get this to run," you're asking "what breaks when you push this a thousand times bigger," and those are the problems I find most interesting. A lot of RL's weaknesses, like instability and sample inefficiency, look very different once you have serious compute and infrastructure behind them.

And third, I liked that research there is tied to something concrete. RL isn't a benchmark exercise, it's part of how the models actually get trained and shipped, through things like RLHF. So when you fix an infrastructure bottleneck or improve an algorithm, you can see it affect a real system that people use. That feedback loop is very motivating for someone who likes both the engineering and the research side.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts OpenAI’s large-scale compute and infrastructure with Weng’s student work on a handful of GPUs, but it does not describe an ad hoc approach at small university research groups or say that Weng hoped to learn a different research methodology.

astra-6.text: For me, the appeal was the chance to work on reinforcement learning in a place where research could connect directly to building useful systems. There are so many interesting questions about how models learn from feedback, and being able to explore those questions alongside people working on different parts of the problem was really exciting. It felt like an opportunity to both deepen my understanding of RL and see where those ideas could make a practical difference.

r001.rationale: The response describes connecting RL research to useful systems, but it does not contrast a methodology she hoped to learn at OpenAI with an ad hoc approach at small university research groups.
